name: Zucchini / Courgette

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Plant zucchini in rich, well-drained soil. Mix a few inches of compost into the bed before you plant, and use raised beds or low mounds if your soil is heavy or stays wet. Good drainage plus plenty of compost gives you healthy, productive plants.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Zucchini grows best in deep, fertile loam that holds steady moisture yet drains freely. Work several inches of compost or well-rotted manure into the bed before planting, since these are organic-matter-hungry plants. Raised beds or mounded hills improve drainage and warm the soil faster in spring. Sandy loams warm early and suit the earliest sowings, while heavy clay holds water and invites root and crown rot, so amend it generously or grow in raised beds.

ph.note_beginner: Zucchini likes soil close to neutral, around pH 6.0 to 6.5, and most garden soil is already in range. If you have never tested your soil, an inexpensive test kit tells you whether you need to adjust it.
ph.note_seasoned: Zucchini does best in slightly acidic to neutral soil, around pH 6.0 to 6.5. It tolerates a wider band, roughly 5.8 to 7.5, and still produces in mildly alkaline soil, though uptake of iron and manganese tightens as pH climbs. A soil test is the only reliable guide before adding lime or sulfur.

fertilizer.example_product: balanced 10-10-10 or compost plus a nitrogen source
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Zucchini is a moderate feeder, hungrier than a light crop like beans but well short of a heavy feeder. The main pitfall is too much nitrogen, which drives lush leaves and shy fruiting, sometimes with poor set. A bed enriched with compost plus one balanced side-dressing as the plant comes into flower is usually all it needs. Pair feeding with steady, even moisture, since the nutrients only help if the plant is not also drought-stressed.
fertilizer.notes_beginner: Zucchini needs a moderate amount of feeding, not a lot. The biggest mistake is too much nitrogen, which gives you big leafy plants but fewer squash. Good compost in the soil plus one feeding when flowers appear is usually enough. Keep the plant evenly watered too, since feeding only helps a well-watered plant.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Your zucchini is coming into flower, time for a single balanced side-dressing. Keep nitrogen moderate so the plant sets fruit instead of running to leaf.
fertilizer.notify_message_beginner: Your zucchini is starting to flower. Give it one feeding of balanced fertilizer now.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits zucchini. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn-type fertilizers, which push foliage at the expense of fruit.
fertilizer.npk_hint_beginner: Use a balanced fertilizer with equal numbers, like 10-10-10. Avoid high-nitrogen lawn fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_seasoned: Work a balanced fertilizer or 1 to 2 inches of compost into the bed before planting, then side-dress once as plants begin to run and flower, roughly 4 to 6 weeks after sowing. A common rate is about 1 tablespoon of 10-10-10 per plant worked into the soil a few inches away from the stem, or a comparable scoop of compost or balanced organic fertilizer.
fertilizer.amount_beginner: Mix some compost or a balanced fertilizer into the soil before planting. Then feed once more when the plants start to flower, about a month after sowing. A spoonful of balanced fertilizer per plant, scratched into the soil a few inches from the stem, is plenty.

companions.note_beginner: Good companions for squash do one of three things: draw pests away, bring in bees, or feed the soil. Plant a few nasturtiums or marigolds nearby to lure squash bugs off your plants, add flowers like borage to attract the bees that pollinate your squash, and let beans share the bed to enrich the soil. Just give your squash plenty of room, since the plants get big.
companions.note_seasoned: Squash benefits most from companions that pull pests away, feed beneficial insects, or fix nitrogen, rather than from plants packed in tight. Give sprawling vines their room and use companions as a border or light interplanting. The strongest evidence is for nasturtium, with marigold close behind, reducing squash bug and cucumber beetle pressure, while the Three Sisters trio (corn, beans, squash) earns its place through nitrogen, support, and pest confusion. Pollinator flowers like borage and sweet alyssum matter because squash is insect-pollinated, so anything that keeps bees working improves fruit set. Several herb and flower pairings here are traditional rather than trial-proven, and are labeled accordingly.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Corn
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Part of the classic Three Sisters planting. The tall stalks support climbing beans, and growing corn, beans, and squash together can confuse squash pests.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Pole beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Beans pull nitrogen from the air and feed the soil, which hungry squash appreciate. Let them climb the corn in a Three Sisters bed.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: These easy flowers lure squash bugs and beetles away from your squash, and research backs it up. Bonus: the flowers are edible.

good_seasoned.name: Corn
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The structural backbone of the Three Sisters. Tall corn gives pole beans a living trellis, and interplanting corn, beans, and squash makes it harder for squash pests to zero in on the planting.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Three Sisters polyculture; corn-as-support and squash-as-groundcover are well established in extension guidance.

good_seasoned.name: Pole beans
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Beans fix atmospheric nitrogen and ease the fertilizer demand of hungry squash, and in a Three Sisters bed they climb the corn while squash shades the soil below.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: Legume nitrogen fixation and Three Sisters companion structure are extension-supported.

good_seasoned.name: Nasturtium
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: The strongest flower pairing for squash: research shows nasturtium can pull squash bugs off the crop, and an Iowa study found it reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage. The flowers are also edible.

provenance.label: research_backed
provenance.reason: UMN states the practice is supported by research; cites an Iowa study on squash bug and cucumber beetle damage.

good_seasoned.name: Marigold
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: Often planted with squash to deter pests. The evidence is mixed overall, but the same Iowa study that backs nasturtium also found marigolds reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage, so it earns a likely rating here.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: UMN reports an Iowa study showing marigolds reduced squash bug and cucumber beetle damage, while noting marigold results are inconsistent generally.

good_seasoned.name: Sweet alyssum
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A low carpet of sweet alyssum draws hoverflies and other beneficial insects. A Florida study found alyssum increased natural enemies of aphids on squash, and the blooms also feed pollinators.

provenance.label: likely
provenance.reason: UMN cites a Florida study in which sweet alyssum increased natural enemies of aphids on squash.

good_seasoned.name: Borage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: A classic pollinator magnet. Its bee-friendly blue flowers help keep pollinators working the squash blooms, which matters because zucchini is insect-pollinated. The pairing is traditional rather than trial-proven.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Well-documented traditional pollinator companion; squash-specific benefit not from a controlled trial.

good_seasoned.name: Sage
good_seasoned.why_seasoned: An aromatic herb long planted near squash to discourage squash bugs. Treat this as traditional garden lore rather than a tested effect for squash.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Aromatic-herb pest-deterrence is widely repeated folk practice; no squash-specific trial support.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Keep potatoes in a separate bed. Both plants are big and hungry and will compete for food and space.

bad_beginner_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_beginner_seasoned.why_beginner: Plant fennel on its own, away from squash. It grows large and may crowd or stunt nearby vegetables.

bad_seasoned.name: Potatoes
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Both potatoes and squash are vigorous, hungry plants that compete hard for the same water, nutrients, and ground space, so most growers keep them in separate beds. The caution is traditional rather than trial-proven.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Widely repeated competition-based caution; not from a controlled companion trial.

bad_seasoned.name: Fennel
bad_seasoned.why_seasoned: Fennel is the classic give-it-its-own-bed plant. It is reputed to release compounds that can suppress nearby vegetables, and it grows large enough to crowd sprawling squash. The allelopathy evidence is mostly observational, so treat this as traditional caution.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Fennel allelopathy toward garden vegetables is largely observational; squash-specific effect uncertain.

pests.name: Squash vine borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of the whole plant or individual vines in midsummer, often after looking healthy. A telltale ring of yellow-orange frass (sawdust-like waste) sits at the base of the stem near a small entry hole.
pests.symptoms_beginner: The plant suddenly wilts in midsummer, even with wet soil. Look for sawdust-like specks at the base of the stem, a sign the borer is inside.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of a clearwing moth tunnel inside the stem, cutting off water flow. The adult lays eggs at the stem base from early to midsummer; the hatching larva bores in and feeds, collapsing the plant.
pests.cause_beginner: A moth lays eggs at the base of the plant in summer. The larvae hatch and tunnel inside the stem, blocking water and killing the plant.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: At the first frass, slit the stem lengthwise with a knife, remove the larva, and mound moist soil over the wound so it can re-root. Promptly remove and destroy plants too far gone.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: If you catch it early, carefully cut a slit in the stem, remove the grub inside, and cover the spot with damp soil. Remove plants that are too damaged.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Time a fall succession to crop after the borer's main flight. Row cover until flowering excludes the egg-laying moth. Wrap the lower stem with foil, scout for eggs from early summer, and remove spent vines to break the cycle.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants until they flower to keep the moth away, and plant a second crop in summer that grows after the borer is gone. Clean up old plants at season's end.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves develop yellow then brown speckling and wilt; heavy infestations cause whole-vine collapse. Look for clusters of bronze, oval eggs on leaf undersides and fast-moving gray-brown nymphs.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Leaves get yellow or brown spots and wilt. Check leaf undersides for shiny bronze eggs in clusters and gray bugs that scatter when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: A shield-shaped true bug that feeds by sucking sap from leaves and stems, injecting toxic saliva. Adults overwinter in garden debris and emerge to lay eggs on cucurbits in early summer.
pests.cause_beginner: A flat, gray bug that sucks sap from the plant and injects damaging saliva. It hides in old plant debris over winter and comes out to lay eggs in summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Crush egg clusters by hand and drop adults and nymphs into soapy water. Lay a board near plants overnight; bugs gather under it and can be collected at dawn. Insecticidal soap works on young nymphs only.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Squash the egg clusters and knock bugs into soapy water. A board left out overnight gives them a hiding spot you can check and clear each morning.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove garden debris where adults overwinter, rotate cucurbits, and use row cover until flowering. Scout leaf undersides for eggs from early summer, before populations explode.
pests.prevention_beginner: Clean up old plant debris, move squash to a new spot each year, and check leaf undersides for eggs through the summer so you can remove them early.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Striped or spotted yellow-and-black beetles chewing leaves, flowers, and young fruit. Seedling damage can be severe, and the beetles transmit bacterial wilt as they feed.
pests.symptoms_beginner: Small yellow beetles with stripes or spots chewing the leaves and flowers. They are most damaging to young plants and can spread disease.
pests.cause_seasoned: Striped and spotted cucumber beetles feed on cucurbits and vector the bacterium that causes bacterial wilt. They overwinter nearby and move onto plants from emergence onward.
pests.cause_beginner: These beetles feed on squash plants and carry bacterial wilt disease, which they pass on as they chew.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick or vacuum beetles in the cool morning, and use yellow sticky traps to monitor. Kaolin clay deters feeding. Protecting seedlings matters most, since young plants and wilt transmission are the real risks.
pests.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick beetles off by hand in the morning when they are slow. Yellow sticky traps help you track them. Protecting young plants is the most important step.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row cover until flowering keeps beetles off vulnerable seedlings (remove for pollination). Rotate cucurbits and clear debris. Wilt-resistant practices matter more than killing every beetle.
pests.prevention_beginner: Cover young plants until they flower to keep beetles off, then remove the cover for the bees. Rotate crops and clean up debris.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White, powdery patches on leaf surfaces, usually starting on older leaves in mid- to late season, spreading until leaves yellow, brown, and die. Severe defoliation exposes fruit and cuts yield.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: White powdery spots on the leaves, usually later in the season, that spread until leaves dry up and die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A fungal disease favored by warm days, cool nights, and high humidity. Unlike most leaf diseases it does not need leaf wetness to infect, but crowded, poorly ventilated plantings worsen it.
diseases.cause_beginner: A fungus that thrives in warm, humid weather. It spreads fastest on crowded plants with poor air flow.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: At first spots, treat with a labeled fungicide such as potassium bicarbonate, neem, or sulfur (not in high heat), repeating per label. Remove the worst leaves. Treatment slows spread but does not cure infected tissue.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: Treat early spots with an approved fungicide like neem or potassium bicarbonate, and remove the worst leaves. Catching it early works best.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants for airflow, and water at the base to keep humidity around foliage down. Full sun and good spacing matter more than spraying.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Pick mildew-resistant varieties, give plants room to breathe, and water the soil instead of the leaves. Good air flow is the best prevention.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Individual leaves or runners wilt and the whole plant collapses, often with leaves still green. A diagnostic test: cut a wilted stem, press the cut ends together and slowly pull apart, and a sticky white ooze strings between them.
diseases.symptoms_beginner: The plant wilts and dies even though the soil is moist and the leaves still look green. It is caused by a disease beetles carry.
diseases.cause_seasoned: A bacterium that clogs the plant's water-conducting tissue, transmitted by cucumber beetles as they feed. The bacterium overwinters in the beetles, not the soil, so beetle control is disease control.
diseases.cause_beginner: A disease spread by cucumber beetles. It clogs the plant's water system, so controlling the beetles is the way to prevent it.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: There is no cure once a plant is infected. Remove and destroy wilting plants promptly to limit beetle spread to healthy ones.
diseases.organic_treatment_beginner: There is no cure once a plant has it. Pull out and remove affected plants quickly so the disease does not spread.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control cucumber beetles, especially on seedlings: row cover until flowering, scouting, and prompt removal of infected plants. Resistant cucurbit types help where available.
diseases.prevention_beginner: Prevent it by controlling cucumber beetles. Cover young plants until they flower, and remove any plant that wilts and dies suddenly.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Aim for about 1 inch of water per week, more in heat or sandy soil, delivered deeply and less often rather than in light daily sprinkles. Container plants dry out faster and often need water every day or two at peak.
watering.frequency_beginner: Give zucchini about 1 inch of water a week, more when it is hot. Water deeply rather than a little every day. Plants in pots dry out fast and may need water daily in summer.
watering.amount_seasoned: Around 1 inch per week is the baseline, equivalent to roughly two-thirds of a gallon per square foot. Push toward the higher end during fruit set and through hot, dry spells, when uneven water shows up directly in the fruit.
watering.amount_beginner: About 1 inch of water a week is a good target. Water more during hot weather and while the plant is setting and growing fruit.
watering.method_seasoned: Water at the base of the plant with a soaker hose, drip line, or a wand aimed at the soil, keeping the leaves as dry as possible. Wet foliage, especially overhead watering late in the day, invites powdery mildew on a plant already prone to it. A 2 to 3 inch mulch holds soil moisture even and keeps splashing down.
watering.method_beginner: Water the soil, not the leaves. Use a soaker hose or aim a watering wand at the base of the plant. Keeping the leaves dry helps prevent powdery mildew, a common zucchini problem. A layer of mulch keeps the soil evenly moist.
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing lower leaves, wilting even when the soil is wet, and soft or rotting stems at the base point to overwatering or poor drainage. Constantly saturated soil invites root and crown rot, particularly in heavy ground.
watering.signs_overwater_beginner: If lower leaves turn yellow, the plant wilts even though the soil is wet, or the base gets soft and mushy, it is getting too much water or the soil drains poorly.
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Midday wilting that recovers overnight is normal in heat, but leaves that stay limp, dull, and curled signal real drought. The clearest fruit-stage tell is misshapen or pinched squash, often narrow at the blossom end, which traces directly to inadequate or uneven water during sizing.
watering.signs_underwater_beginner: Some midday wilting in hot weather is normal and passes by evening. Leaves that stay wilted mean the plant is too dry. Uneven watering can also make the squash come out misshapen.
watering.method_note_seasoned: Base watering is the single most useful habit for zucchini, because the same plant that wants steady moisture is also one of the most mildew-prone in the garden. Keep water on the soil and air moving through the leaves.
watering.method_note_beginner: Watering the soil instead of the leaves is the best thing you can do for zucchini. It keeps the plant hydrated without encouraging leaf disease.
watering.critical_periods_seasoned: The water-critical stretch is flowering through fruit set and sizing. Steady moisture here is what produces well-formed fruit; let it swing dry and you get poor set and pinched, misshapen squash even with good pollination.
watering.critical_periods_beginner: The most important time to keep zucchini watered is when it is flowering and forming fruit. Even watering then gives you well-shaped squash.

start_method.hardening_off_seasoned: Harden off indoor-started squash over 7 to 10 days, easing them into direct sun and wind before transplanting. Handle the rootball gently at planting, because squash resents root disturbance and a checked seedling can sulk for weeks.
start_method.hardening_off_beginner: If you started seedlings indoors, set them outside for a little longer each day over about a week so they adjust to sun and wind. Be gentle with the roots when you plant, since squash does not like having its roots disturbed.
start_method.notes_seasoned: Because squash resents root disturbance, direct sowing once the soil warms past 60°F, ideally 70°F, is the simplest and most reliable method, and direct-sown plants quickly catch up to transplants. Start seeds indoors only to gain two to three weeks in a short season, using larger cells (3 inch or bigger) and setting plants out before the roots circle the pot.
start_method.notes_beginner: The easiest way to grow zucchini is to sow seeds right where they will grow, once the soil is warm (about 70°F). Squash grows fast and does not transplant happily, so direct sowing usually works best. Start seeds indoors only if your season is short, and move them outside while they are still small.

container_notes.shape_requirements: Zucchini is a big, sprawling plant with a deep root system, so it needs a wide, deep container, at least 12 inches deep and a 10 gallon or larger pot for a full-size variety. Wide and sturdy beats tall and narrow, since a top-heavy plant in a small pot tips and dries out fast. Compact and bush varieties are far happier in containers than sprawling heirlooms.

drainage.saucer_practice: If you use a saucer, empty it after watering. Zucchini will not tolerate sitting in standing water, which invites root and crown rot.

soil_mix.type_beginner: Use a good bagged potting mix, not soil from the garden. Garden soil packs down too hard in a pot.
soil_mix.amendments_beginner: Mix in some compost, and add a slow-release fertilizer when you plant. Pots need feeding more often than garden beds because watering washes nutrients out.
soil_mix.type_seasoned: Use a high-quality peat- or coir-based potting mix, not garden soil, which compacts and drains poorly in a container. The mix should be rich but free-draining.
soil_mix.amendments_seasoned: Blend in about a third compost for fertility and a handful of a slow-release balanced fertilizer at planting. Because frequent watering flushes nutrients from a pot, plan to feed more regularly than you would in the ground.

container_notes.watering_adjustment_beginner: Pots dry out much faster than garden beds. In summer you may need to water a potted zucchini every day, sometimes twice. Check daily and water until it drains from the bottom.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_beginner: Feed potted zucchini more often than garden plants. After planting, give a balanced liquid feed every couple of weeks once it starts flowering.

overwintering.approach_beginner: Not applicable. Zucchini lives for one season and dies with the first frost, so you cannot overwinter it. Just plant new seeds next year.
overwintering.approach_seasoned: Not applicable. Zucchini is a frost-tender annual that completes its life in a single season and is killed by the first hard frost, so there is nothing to overwinter. Pull spent plants at season's end and start fresh from seed the following year.

container_notes.notes_beginner: You can grow zucchini in a container, but it needs a big pot, at least 10 gallons and 12 inches deep, and a compact variety works best. Put it in full sun, keep it well watered (pots dry out fast), and feed it regularly. Water the soil, not the leaves, to help avoid mildew.
container_notes.notes_seasoned: Zucchini is growable in containers but demands a big one: a 10 gallon or larger pot at least 12 inches deep, and ideally a compact or bush variety such as Raven, Astia, Bush Baby, Patio Star, or Eight Ball rather than a sprawling heirloom. The main container challenges are water and feeding, since pots dry and deplete fast, plus the same powdery mildew and pollination issues as in the ground. Give it full sun, water at the base daily in heat, and feed regularly.
container_notes.watering_adjustment_seasoned: Containers dry out far faster than beds, and a large zucchini in a pot can need water once or even twice a day in summer heat. Check daily by feeling the top inch of mix, and water until it runs from the drainage holes. Self-watering or larger pots buffer the swings that cause misshapen fruit.
container_notes.fertilizer_adjustment_seasoned: Feed container plants more often than in-ground ones, since watering steadily leaches nutrients. After the slow-release charge at planting, add a balanced liquid feed every 2 to 3 weeks once flowering begins, keeping nitrogen moderate.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_seasoned: Zucchini does well in self-watering containers, which smooth out the moisture swings this thirsty, mildew-prone plant dislikes. Keep the reservoir topped up in heat and still water from below, leaving the foliage dry, and use a large enough planter that the root mass is not constantly waterlogged.
container_notes.self_watering_notes_beginner: Self-watering pots work well for zucchini because they keep moisture steady. Keep the water reservoir filled, especially in hot weather, and use a good-sized pot.

recommended.name: Black Beauty
recommended.recommended_note: Classic dark-green heirloom; compact, open-pollinated, and dependably productive.

recommended.name: Costata Romanesco
recommended.recommended_note: Ribbed Italian heirloom prized for nutty flavor; large, sprawling plants that reward room.

recommended.name: Raven
recommended.recommended_note: Compact dark-green hybrid that suits containers and small beds.

recommended.name: Goldrush
recommended.recommended_note: Bright golden-yellow hybrid with uniform, easy-to-spot fruit.

recommended.name: Cocozelle
recommended.recommended_note: Striped Italian heirloom with firm, flavorful fruit.

recommended.name: Dunja
recommended.recommended_note: Vigorous organic hybrid with an open, easy-to-pick habit.

varieties.note_seasoned: For a first garden almost any zucchini succeeds, so choose by space and color. Compact bush habits like Raven or Dunja fit small beds and containers and keep airflow open to slow powdery mildew, while sprawling heirlooms like Costata Romanesco and Cocozelle reward more room with exceptional flavor. Mixing a green type with a yellow one such as Goldrush makes fruit easier to spot before it oversizes. Black Beauty remains the reliable green standard.
varieties.note_beginner: Zucchini is forgiving, so pick a variety by the space you have. Bush types like Raven stay compact and do well in pots, while classics like Black Beauty are reliable in a garden bed. A yellow type such as Goldrush is easy to spot at picking size.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Avoid planting zucchini where another cucurbit grew last year, including cucumber, melon, pumpkin, winter squash, and other summer squash. They share squash bug, squash vine borer, cucumber beetle, and soilborne diseases that build up in the soil and on debris.
rotation.avoid_after_beginner: Do not plant zucchini where you grew cucumbers, melons, pumpkins, or other squash last year. They get the same pests and diseases, which build up in the soil.
rotation.good_after: Legumes (beans and peas), leafy greens, or alliums (onions and garlic) make good preceding crops, since they do not share the cucurbit pest and disease complex; a legume also leaves nitrogen behind.
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate cucurbits on a 2 to 3 year cycle, returning zucchini to a given bed no sooner than the third year. The point is to break the buildup of squash bug, vine borer, and soilborne disease. Clearing spent vines at season's end, rather than tilling them in, removes overwintering sites and makes rotation more effective.
rotation.note_beginner: Try not to grow zucchini or its relatives in the same spot more than once every 3 years. Moving it around the garden each year helps avoid a buildup of pests and disease. Clean up old plants at the end of the season too.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Summer squash is tender and short-lived off the plant. At room temperature it keeps only a couple of days before softening, so refrigerate soon after picking unless you will use it right away.
storage.room_temp_beginner: Zucchini does not keep long at room temperature, just a day or two. Put it in the fridge if you are not using it right away.
storage.fridge_seasoned: Stored unwashed in a perforated or loosely closed bag in the crisper, zucchini keeps about 1 week, sometimes a few days more. It is chilling-sensitive below about 41°F, where prolonged cold causes pitting and soft spots, so it does not store as long or as cold as hardy vegetables.
storage.fridge_beginner: Keep zucchini in the fridge in a loosely closed bag for about a week. Do not wash it until you are ready to use it.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Zucchini does not freeze well raw, turning watery and limp, but freezes fine for cooking when shredded or sliced and blanched briefly first. Shredded zucchini, drained and frozen in measured portions, is ideal for breads and soups later.
storage.freezer_beginner: Zucchini freezes best shredded or sliced and quickly blanched first, then frozen for cooking later. Frozen raw, it turns watery, so it is best used in cooked dishes, not eaten fresh.
storage.notes_seasoned: Treat zucchini as a use-it-soon vegetable rather than a keeper. The practical answer to a glut is not long storage but cooking, giving it away, and freezing shredded squash for winter baking.
storage.notes_beginner: Zucchini is best used fresh and soon after picking. If you have too much, the best options are to cook it, share it, or freeze it shredded for later.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprout in about 5 to 10 days in warm soil (70 to 95°F is ideal); cold soil below 60°F rots seed rather than germinating it.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: In warm soil, seeds sprout in about a week. Two seed leaves push up first. If the soil is cold, seeds rot instead of sprouting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow 1 inch deep in warm soil. Keep evenly moist, not soggy. If you sowed several seeds per spot, thin to the strongest seedling once true leaves appear.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Plant seeds 1 inch deep once the soil is warm. Keep the soil damp until they sprout. If several come up together, keep the strongest one.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Did your zucchini seeds germinate, and how many days did it take?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cotyledons followed by the first true leaves; growth is fast once warm. Watch for cucumber beetles, which target young plants and can transmit bacterial wilt.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: After the first two rounded leaves, true leaves appear and the plant grows quickly. Watch for beetles chewing the young leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Protect from cucumber beetles, with row cover if needed (remove it at flowering for pollination). Keep evenly watered and free of weeds.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Keep an eye out for beetles on young plants. Water regularly and keep weeds down. A light row cover can protect seedlings, but remove it once flowers form.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How are your seedlings developing? Any sign of beetle damage?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: How do your young plants look?

growth_stages.name: Established and vining
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Rapid leafy growth and a thickening main stem as the plant bulks up before flowering. This is the window to side-dress and the time squash vine borer moths begin laying eggs at the stem base.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant grows fast, with big leaves and a thick stem, getting ready to flower. This is when you feed it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Side-dress once with balanced fertilizer. Mulch to hold moisture. Begin scouting the stem base for squash vine borer eggs and frass, especially from early summer.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Give the plant one feeding of balanced fertilizer now. Add mulch to keep the soil moist. Start checking the base of the stem for pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Has your zucchini been side-dressed? Any pests at the stem base?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large yellow flowers. Male flowers (on thin stalks) usually open first and may drop before females appear, which is normal; female flowers carry a tiny squash behind the bloom.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Big yellow flowers open. The first flowers are usually male and fall off, which is normal. Female flowers have a tiny squash at their base.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Encourage pollinators and avoid spraying open blooms. If small fruit yellow and rot at the tip, pollination is poor, hand-pollinate with a small brush in the morning. Keep moisture steady now.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Let the bees do their work and do not spray the flowers. If tiny squash turn yellow and rot, the flowers were not pollinated, you can hand-pollinate with a small brush. Keep watering steadily.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are you seeing female flowers and fruit set? Any blossom-end rot on small fruit?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant flowering? Are any little squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Glossy fruit reaching pickable size (6 to 8 inches for standard types), sizing up fast, often an inch or more per day at peak.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: Shiny squash reaching about 6 to 8 inches. They grow fast, so they are ready before you expect.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 1 to 2 days, cutting the stem with a knife. Harvest young for tenderness and to keep the plant producing; remove any oversized fruit you missed.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Check every day or two and pick the squash while they are still small and shiny. Cut the stem with a knife. Picking often keeps more coming.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How much are you harvesting, and how often are you picking?

growth_stages.name: End of season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Declining production, increasing powdery mildew, or sudden wilting from squash vine borer or bacterial wilt. The first frost kills the plant outright.
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_beginner: The plant slows down and leaves may get powdery and white, or it wilts suddenly from pests. Frost kills it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pull and remove spent plants rather than tilling them in, to cut overwintering pest and disease sites. A summer-sown succession often crops cleanly after the first planting fades.
growth_stages.user_action_beginner: Pull out finished plants and clear them away at the end of the season. This helps prevent pests next year. A second planting made in summer often keeps producing after the first one is done.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Is this planting winding down? Did you remove the spent plants?
growth_stages.log_prompt_beginner: Is your plant finished for the season?

notifications.title_seasoned: Start scouting for squash vine borer
notifications.title_beginner: Time to watch for stem pests
notifications.body_seasoned: Your zucchini is bulking up, which is when squash vine borer moths lay eggs at the stem base. Check the base of the stem for sawdust-like frass from now through midsummer, and act early if you see it.
notifications.body_beginner: Your zucchini is growing fast now. Check the bottom of the stem for sawdust-like specks, an early sign of a borer, and keep checking through summer.

notifications.body_seasoned: Time to sow a succession planting. A fresh sowing now, counted back from your first fall frost, often outproduces the spring crop on cleaner plants once borer and mildew wear the first planting down.
notifications.body_beginner: Now is a good time to plant a second zucchini as a backup. Pests often wear out the first plants by late summer, so a fresh planting keeps squash coming.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your zucchini, it sizes up fast
notifications.body_seasoned: Your zucchini is fruiting. At peak it can gain an inch a day, so check every 1 to 2 days and pick young at 6 to 8 inches. Frequent picking keeps the plant producing.
notifications.body_beginner: Your zucchini is making fruit. Check every day or two and pick them while small and shiny, they grow fast.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost is coming, zucchini will not survive it
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A frost is forecast. Zucchini is frost-tender and the first frost ends the plant, so pick everything usable now. There is no covering that reliably carries a large squash plant through a freeze.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Frost is coming, and it will kill your zucchini. Pick all the squash you can use before it hits.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Extreme heat may stall fruit set
weather_triggers.title_beginner: Hot spell may slow your squash
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A stretch of extreme heat is forecast. Very hot days can reduce pollination and fruit set temporarily, sometimes dropping young fruit. Keep moisture steady; set usually resumes when the heat eases.
weather_triggers.body_beginner: Very hot weather is coming. Your zucchini may slow down or drop small fruit for a while. Keep it well watered, it usually picks back up when it cools.

germination.text_seasoned: Soil temperature, not the calendar, governs zucchini germination. Wait until soil is at least 70°F at 2 inches; seed sown in cold ground rots before it sprouts.
germination.text_beginner: Wait for warm soil before sowing. Zucchini seeds rot in cold ground but sprout fast once it warms up.

seedling.text_seasoned: Cucumber beetles swarm young squash and can spread bacterial wilt. A floating row cover protects seedlings, but pull it off at flowering so bees can pollinate.
seedling.text_beginner: Protect young plants from beetles. A light cover helps, but take it off once flowers appear so bees can reach them.

established.text_seasoned: This is the one feeding zucchini needs: a single balanced side-dressing as the plant bulks up and starts to run. Resist piling on nitrogen, which gives leaves at the expense of fruit.
established.text_beginner: Feed the plant once now, as it gets big and starts to flower. Do not overdo the fertilizer, too much makes leaves instead of squash.

established.text_seasoned: Start scouting the stem base for squash vine borer from early summer. A ring of frass (sawdust-like waste) at the base is the early warning before the wilt.
established.text_beginner: Check the bottom of the stem for pests starting in early summer. Look for sawdust-like specks, an early sign of a borer.

flowering.text_seasoned: Early male flowers opening and dropping with no fruit is normal; females come a little later. Judge pollination by whether small fruit size up or yellow and rot at the blossom end.
flowering.text_beginner: The first flowers often fall off without making squash, that is normal. Real trouble is when tiny squash turn yellow and rot, which means poor pollination.

flowering.text_seasoned: If set is poor in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions, hand-pollinate in the morning: pick a male flower, strip the petals, and dab pollen onto the center of each open female.
flowering.text_beginner: If squash are not forming, you can hand-pollinate. In the morning, pick a male flower, peel off the petals, and gently touch it to the center of a female flower.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick young and pick often. At peak, fruit can gain an inch a day, so check every 1 to 2 days, and harvesting promptly keeps the plant setting new fruit instead of slowing down.
harvest.text_beginner: Pick zucchini while small and check every day or two, they grow fast. Picking often keeps more squash coming.

harvest.text_seasoned: Missed a fruit and it turned into a marrow? Cut it off and compost or use it anyway; leaving mature, seedy fruit on the plant suppresses further production.
harvest.text_beginner: If a squash got huge, pick it off anyway, even if you do not use it. Leaving big squash on the plant makes it stop producing.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Pull spent vines and remove them rather than tilling them under, which buries overwintering squash bugs and disease. Clean beds now mean fewer pests next season.
end_of_season.text_beginner: At the end of the season, pull up old plants and clear them away. This cuts down on pests and disease next year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A healthy plant yields heavily, commonly 6 to 10 pounds of fruit over a season, often more in a long, warm climate. Two plants are plenty for most households, and a single plant at peak can produce more than one family can eat.
yield_expectations.per_plant_beginner: One zucchini plant produces a lot, usually several pounds over the season. One or two plants are plenty for most families.
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: At peak in warm weather a plant can set new fruit daily, and squash sizes up so fast that picking every 1 to 2 days is essential. Frequent harvest at this stage actually keeps the plant producing; leaving mature fruit on the vine signals it to slow down.
yield_expectations.peak_production_beginner: At its peak, a zucchini plant makes squash incredibly fast. Pick every day or two, picking often actually keeps more squash coming.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Zucchini is forgiving and productive even for a first-time grower; the usual first-year surprise is not too little but too much. Plant only one or two, and be ready to pick constantly once it gets going.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_beginner: Zucchini is one of the easiest crops for beginners, and the usual surprise is how much you get. Start with just one or two plants.
factors_seasoned: Pollination: poor pollination in cool or pollinator-scarce conditions cuts yield and causes blossom-end rot of small fruit.
Harvest frequency: picking young and often keeps a plant productive; letting fruit mature slows new set.
Pest and disease pressure: squash vine borer and powdery mildew commonly end the first planting by midsummer.
Even moisture: steady water through fruit set drives well-formed fruit and sustained production.
Season length and heat: long warm seasons extend the productive window; a frost ends it.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: No T1 source supports timing zucchini planting by moon phase. We do not make a recommendation here; sow by soil temperature and frost dates instead.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Small fruit yellowed and rotted at the blossom end
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Tiny squash turned yellow and rotted
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Poor pollination. The female flower was not adequately pollinated, so the young fruit aborts, yellowing and rotting at the blossom end instead of sizing up. Common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: The flower was not pollinated well, so the little squash died instead of growing. This often happens in cool or rainy weather, or when there are few bees.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Inadequate transfer of pollen to the female flower, often compounded by early-season timing before pollinator activity peaks.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not enough pollination of the flower.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant flowers to draw pollinators, avoid spraying open blooms, and hand-pollinate in the morning if early set is poor. It usually improves as more flowers open and bees get active.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Grow some flowers nearby for the bees, and hand-pollinate early squash if needed. It usually gets better as the season goes on.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Squash hidden under leaves until it was a giant marrow
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Found a giant zucchini you missed
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fruit grows fast and hides under the large leaves, so a missed squash becomes an oversized, seedy, tough-skinned marrow within days. Mature fruit left on the plant also slows new production.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Zucchini grows so fast it hides under the leaves and gets huge in just a few days. Big squash are tough and seedy, and leaving them on slows the plant down.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Infrequent harvest combined with dense foliage; fruit can gain an inch or more a day at peak.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: Not picking often enough while squash grow very fast.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check plants every 1 to 2 days at peak, lifting leaves to find hidden fruit, and pick young. Remove any marrows you find to keep the plant cropping.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Check every day or two and look under the leaves. Pick squash small, and remove any big ones to keep more coming.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Healthy plant wilted and collapsed in midsummer
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most likely squash vine borer: a larva tunneled into the stem and cut off water, collapsing a previously vigorous plant in mid- to late summer. Look for frass at the stem base. Bacterial wilt (beetle-vectored) causes similar sudden collapse.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Usually a squash vine borer, a grub that tunnels into the stem and kills the plant in summer. Look for sawdust-like specks at the base. Beetle-spread bacterial wilt can look similar.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Squash vine borer larva inside the stem, or bacterial wilt clogging the water-conducting tissue.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A borer inside the stem, or a disease spread by beetles.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Use row cover until flowering, scout the stem base for frass from early summer, and time a fall succession to crop after the borer's flight. Remove spent vines at season's end.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Cover plants until they flower, check the stem base for pests, and plant a second crop in summer as a backup. Clean up old plants at the end of the season.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Leaves turned white and powdery, then the plant faded early
failure_diagnostics.label_beginner: Leaves got white and powdery and the plant died back
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew defoliated the plant ahead of schedule. The white fungal coating spread across the leaves until they browned and died, cutting the productive season short and exposing fruit to sunscald.
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_beginner: Powdery mildew, a white coating on the leaves, spread until the leaves died and the plant stopped early.
failure_diagnostics.cause_seasoned: Powdery mildew fungus, worsened by crowding, poor airflow, and high humidity around the foliage.
failure_diagnostics.cause_beginner: A fungus that spreads on crowded plants with poor air flow.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties, space plants generously, water at the base, and treat at the first spots. A summer-sown succession can carry harvest past the worst of it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_beginner: Pick resistant varieties, give plants more room, water the soil not the leaves, and treat early spots. A second planting helps too.

primary.name: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
UF/IFAS Northwest District Horticulture Vegetable Garden Planting Dates (Florida Panhandle)
UF/IFAS SP 103/VH021 Florida Vegetable Gardening Guide
UGA Extension Bulletin 577 (Vegetable Garden Planting Chart)

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Zucchini is famous for overwhelming a garden, so resist sowing the whole crop at once. A first sowing after your last frost, then a second about three weeks later, spreads the harvest and keeps vigorous plants coming as the originals tire. The real payoff is late season: squash vine borer and powdery mildew often take down the first planting by midsummer, so a replacement sown in early to midsummer, counting back from your first fall frost so it has time to mature, frequently outproduces the spring crop on cleaner, less stressed plants.
succession_policy.tip_beginner: You rarely need more than one or two zucchini plants at a time, and a single planting can feed you for weeks. For a steadier supply, sow a few seeds now and a few more about three weeks later. A second planting in summer is a smart backup, since pests and disease often wear out the first plants by late summer.

northern_tier.plantings_provenance: Author-fresh from T1 (no legacy zones{} to de-multiplex). Direct-sow-dominant cucurbit: plant_out is the after-frost direct-sow window once soil >=70F at 2 in (UMN); start_indoors is the 3-week transplant-early lead used at the short-season cold end (z3-z5) to gain time. Single continuous summer window capped by the fall-frost runway; succession is the 3-week cadence (UMD/UMN), not a spring/fall split. Fall replacement (squash vine borer / powdery mildew) sits inside the same continuous window, counted back from first frost. Region-specific window per A5; not analogized from another region.
northern_tier.region_notes_beginner: In cold northern areas, zucchini is a summer crop. Wait until after your last frost and the soil has warmed before sowing seeds outside, usually late spring to early summer. If your summers are short, you can start a few seeds indoors about 3 weeks early and move them out gently. For a steady supply, sow a few seeds, then a few more about 3 weeks later. A second planting in summer is a good backup since pests often slow the first plants by late summer.
northern_tier.region_notes_seasoned: Across the cold northern tier (zones 3 to 7) zucchini is a single continuous summer crop, bracketed by frost on both ends. Direct sow after the last frost once the soil reaches about 70°F at 2 inches, which is the reliable trigger here; in the shortest-season zones (3 to 5) you can start seeds indoors roughly 3 weeks ahead and transplant carefully to gain time. There is no spring-and-fall split, just one warm window, so space sowings about 3 weeks apart through early summer for a steady supply. Count any midsummer replacement planting back from your first fall frost so it has time to mature, since squash vine borer and powdery mildew often wear out the first planting by then.

se_gulf.region_notes_beginner: In the Southeast and Gulf, zucchini grows in two seasons: spring and fall, with a break in the hottest part of summer. Plant in spring once frost has passed, then plant again in late summer for a fall crop. Skip the peak of summer, when heat and pests make squash struggle. A spring sowing plus a second one a couple of weeks later gives you a good early supply.
se_gulf.region_notes_seasoned: In the Southeast and Gulf (zones 8 to 9) zucchini is a true spring-and-fall crop with a hot midsummer gap. Sow in spring from about April, making a second sowing 2 to 3 weeks later, then stop: virus pressure, squash vine borer, and heat curtail production through the worst of summer. Sow again for fall by late August so plants establish before cooling weather. The exact dates shift within the region, earlier in spring and later in fall toward south Georgia, the reverse toward the cooler northern edge. The midsummer stretch is a deliberate no-plant gap, not a growing month.
se_gulf.plantings_provenance: UGA Extension Bulletin 577 home-garden planting chart (Squash, bush, 50-55 days: spring Apr 1-May 15, fall Aug 1-20, middle Georgia) plus Circular 943 (make a second planting 2-3 weeks after the first in spring; plant cucumbers and squash for fall no later than Aug 31). The Southeast/Gulf is a true SPRING + FALL split: virus pressure, squash vine borer, and mid-summer heat curtail production in late summer, leaving a no-plant gap between the spring crop's heat-driven end and the fall sowing. The chart's own zone notes shift the dates (south Georgia ~ z9 earlier in spring/later in fall; north-Georgia edge ~ z8 later in spring/earlier in fall). succession_spring + succession_fall per second_planting spec v1.1; the mid-summer no-plant month renders heat_pause. Region-specific per A5; the fall window is a SE finding and is NOT carried to ca_interior or warm_arid.

9.succession_continuous: Mar 15, Apr 5, Apr 26, May 17, Jun 7, Jun 28

ca_interior.region_notes_beginner: In California's inland valleys, zucchini grows right through the warm season in one long stretch. Sow seeds once the soil is warm, from around mid-March into early summer. Hot summer weather is fine, zucchini loves the heat. Production slows in fall as pests build up. Sow a few seeds every few weeks for a steady supply.
ca_interior.region_notes_seasoned: In California's interior valleys (zones 8 to 9) zucchini runs as one long, continuous warm-season crop rather than a spring-and-fall split. Direct sow once the soil warms to about 70°F, safely from roughly mid-March, with set-out continuing into July. Because zucchini is heat-loving, peak summer is the productive core here, not a pause, though production tapers in fall as aphid-transmitted virus and whitefly build up. Space sowings about 3 weeks apart for a steady run, and favor a later planting to carry harvest into the cleaner fall weather.
ca_interior.plantings_provenance: UC ANR Pub 7245 (Summer Squash Production in California) plus Sacramento and Santa Clara/Marin County Master Gardener charts: Central Valley squash is direct-sown once soil reaches ~70 degrees F (Mar 15 safe without protection; soil-warm late Mar through July set-out), producing through summer and tapering in fall on aphid-transmitted virus and whitefly pressure. This is one continuous warm-season window, not a spring/fall split: no mid-summer no-plant gap is documented, and zucchini is heat-loving, so peak heat is a window edge, not a heat_pause. succession_continuous per second_planting spec v1.1 (window_type continuous). Region-specific per A5.

ca_north_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's cool north coast, zucchini grows all season in one stretch, but it gets going later than in hotter areas because of the cool ocean air. Start seeds indoors in March and plant out once nights are reliably mild, from mid-April into June. Harvest continues well into fall. Give plants a warm, sunny spot to make the most of the cooler climate.
ca_north_coast.region_notes_seasoned: On California's cool north coast (zones 9 to 10) the marine layer makes zucchini heat-limited rather than heat-stalled: it grows in one continuous window but starts later and blooms more slowly than inland. Start seeds indoors in March and set plants out from mid-April through June, or even July, once nights stay above about 55°F. Harvest carries late, into fall, as the season cools gradually. There is no midsummer gap here; the limit is cool air, not heat.
ca_north_coast.plantings_provenance: UC Marin Master Gardener squash guide plus UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (North/North Coast column): on the cool maritime coast squash is seeded indoors in March and set out from mid-April through June (some to July), once nights are above 55 degrees F, and bears until weather cools in fall. The marine layer makes this region heat-LIMITED (a later start, a slower bloom), not heat-stalled, so there is no heat_pause and the window is one continuous run. succession_continuous. Region-specific per A5; the coastal behavior is the inverse of ca_interior at the same hardiness band.

ca_south_coast.region_notes_beginner: On California's mild south coast, zucchini grows in one long warm-season stretch from spring into late fall. Wait until the soil is warm, around late April, before planting out. Harvest continues until the weather cools. Even with mild winters, zucchini is killed by frost and slows in the cool season, so it is a warm-weather crop, not year-round.
ca_south_coast.region_notes_seasoned: California's mild south coast (zones 9 to 10) supports one long continuous warm-season window from spring set-out into late fall. Wait for warm soil, roughly late April, before setting plants out, and harvest can run until weather cools. The marine influence limits peak heat rather than forcing a midsummer pause, so this is a single run, not a spring-and-fall split. Despite the mild winters zucchini is still a frost-tender annual with a clear cool-season slowdown; it is not a year-round crop here.
ca_south_coast.plantings_provenance: UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (South Coast column) plus Los Angeles County Master Gardener guidance (wait until warm soil, roughly end of April, to set out squash): the mild South Coast supports one long continuous warm-season window from spring set-out into late fall, heat-limited by the marine layer rather than stalled. No heat_pause; not year_round (a frost-tender annual with a cool-season slowdown). succession_continuous. Region-specific per A5.

ca_desert.region_notes_beginner: In California's low desert, zucchini grows in two seasons around the extreme summer heat. Plant an early crop in late winter or early spring, before it gets hot. Skip the peak of summer, when squash cannot set fruit well. Then plant again in early fall. Getting plants established before the heat is the key to a good spring crop.
ca_desert.region_notes_seasoned: California's low desert (zones 9 to 10, Imperial and Coachella) is a spring-and-fall crop split by a summer too hot for reliable fruit set and heavy with whitefly and virus. Sow an early-spring crop well before the heat, from about February, with the southern desert valleys able to sow as early as December and January. Then stop through the worst of summer and sow again for a fall crop in September. The midsummer months are a deliberate no-plant gap, not growing time.
ca_desert.plantings_provenance: UC ANR Pub 7245 (early-spring desert squash is sown in the cool early months -- the publication notes December and January sowings for the southern desert valleys -- with main production in spring and acreage falling off sharply in fall under aphid-transmitted virus and silverleaf whitefly) plus UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2 (Desert Valleys column, Imperial/Coachella). The low desert is a SPRING + FALL split: an early-spring crop set before the heat, a summer too hot for reliable fruit set and heavy with whitefly/virus, then a fall crop. succession_spring + succession_fall; the mid-summer no-plant months render heat_pause. Region-specific per A5; distinct from low_desert_az (AZ) by institution and by slightly milder z10 timing.

warm_arid.region_label: Warm Arid: Southern New Mexico & West Texas
warm_arid.region_notes_beginner: In the warm, dry band of southern New Mexico and west Texas, zucchini grows in one long warm-season stretch. Sow seeds once the soil is warm after the spring frost, from around April into June. This higher-elevation area does not need the summer break that the low desert does, so you can keep sowing every few weeks for a steady supply through the season.
warm_arid.region_notes_seasoned: The warm arid band of southern New Mexico and west Texas (zone 8) sits higher than the Sonoran low desert, and zucchini runs as one long warm-season window from after the spring frost through to the fall frost. Direct sow once the soil warms, from about April, with set-out continuing into June, and space sowings roughly 3 weeks apart. Unlike the low desert, no midsummer no-plant gap is documented for this elevation, so it is grown as a single continuous run rather than a spring-and-fall split.
warm_arid.plantings_provenance: NMSU Circular 457 statewide planting-date table (southern band, Las Cruces/Dona Ana ~ zone 8) plus Texas A&M AgriLife far-west Texas guidance: the southern New Mexico / west Texas warm-arid band at zone 8 (higher elevation than the Sonoran low desert) runs one long warm-season window after the spring frost through to the fall frost. Unlike the low desert (AZ1005, two short seasons around a brutal summer gap), no T1 documents a mid-summer no-plant break for this higher-elevation z8 band, so it is authored continuous, mirroring the green-beans warm_arid z8 finding. succession_continuous. Region-specific per A5. FLAG: if the release-lane NMSU read shows a desert-style summer no-plant gap at z8, this would split; authored continuous on the evidence in hand.

low_desert_az.region_notes_beginner: In Arizona's low desert, zucchini grows in two seasons with a long break for the extreme summer heat. Plant in late winter to early spring, before it gets hot, and again in late summer for a fall crop. Skip the middle of summer entirely. Getting plants going early, before the heat arrives, makes the biggest difference for the spring crop.
low_desert_az.region_notes_seasoned: Arizona's low desert (zone 9, Maricopa and Yuma) grows zucchini in two distinct seasons around a summer too hot for fruit set and heavy with whitefly. Sow a spring crop from about mid-February through March, extendable toward mid-April if plants establish before the heat, then stop. Sow again for fall from mid-August to mid-September. The long May-to-August stretch is a deliberate no-plant gap; few annuals thrive through the desert summer extreme.
low_desert_az.plantings_provenance: U of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005 (Vegetable Planting Calendar for Maricopa County, peer-reviewed): Summer Squash (60-90 days) is seeded in two distinct seasons -- spring (~Feb 15-Mar 15, extendable to mid-April per the UA low-desert summer-survival guidance if established before the heat) and fall (~Aug 15-Sep 15) -- around a summer too hot for fruit set and heavy with whitefly. AZ1005 states the low desert has two optimal planting seasons (spring and fall) because few annuals thrive through the summer extreme; the cucurbit rows (cucumber, summer squash) show exactly this split. AZ1615 (Yuma) corroborates the two short production windows. succession_spring + succession_fall; the May-Aug no-plant stretch renders heat_pause. Region-specific per A5; zone 9 only (the desert fold at z10 is served by ca_desert).

fl_peninsula.region_notes_beginner: In peninsular Florida, the seasons are flipped: zucchini grows through the cooler months, from late summer through winter and into spring, and takes the summer off. Plant from about mid-August onward, and keep sowing through the mild winter for a steady supply. Skip the hot, humid summer, when squash will not grow well.
fl_peninsula.region_notes_seasoned: On the Florida peninsula (zones 10 to 11) the growing season is inverted: the cool half of the year, roughly late summer through spring, is the continuous window for zucchini, and the June-to-August heat is the off-season. Sow from about mid-August through the mild winter and into early spring, spacing sowings for a steady supply. Summer squash simply does not grow through Florida's peak summer heat and humidity, so those months are a planned break rather than growing time.

hawaii_tropical.region_notes_beginner: In Hawaii, zucchini can grow through much of the year since there is no frost. It does best at cooler elevations and in drier spots. The main challenge is disease and insects during wet weather rather than cold. Plant in the drier months when you can, in a spot with good air movement, and sow every few weeks for a steady supply.
hawaii_tropical.region_notes_seasoned: In Hawaii (zone 11) zucchini can be grown through much of the year, favored at cooler elevations and on drier leeward sites. There is no frost to bracket the season; the practical limiter is wet-season disease and insect pressure rather than cold. Sow across most of the year and space sowings for a steady supply, choosing the drier months and airier sites where you can. Treat it as a long, near-continuous window shaped by rainfall and pests, not by temperature.

description_seasoned: Zucchini is a warm-season summer squash grown for its tender, immature fruit, harvested young before the skin hardens and the seeds mature. Plants are bushy rather than vining, fast from seed, and famously productive: a single plant in good soil can outpace a household at peak. It is monoecious, carrying separate male and female flowers on the same plant, so one plant sets fruit on its own with insect pollination. The two beats that shape a season are pests and pace. Squash vine borer and powdery mildew commonly take down a first planting by midsummer, which is why a second sowing pays off, and fruit sizes up so fast that picking every day or two at peak is the difference between tender squash and baseball-bat marrows.
description_beginner: Zucchini is one of the easiest and most productive vegetables you can grow. It is a bushy summer squash that grows fast from seed and gives you tender squash all summer. One or two plants are usually plenty for a household. Each plant makes both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit, and bees do the rest. The main things to know: pick the squash while it is still small and glossy, check the plants every day or two at peak, and keep an eye out for pests later in the season.
harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick zucchini young, at 6 to 8 inches long for a standard variety, while the skin is glossy and a thumbnail still dents it easily. Round and patty types are best harvested small as well, roughly tennis-ball to softball size. Fruit sizes up fast in warm weather, often gaining an inch or more a day at peak, so check plants every one to two days. Cut the stem with a knife or shears rather than twisting, leaving a short stub of stem on the fruit. Left too long, squash turns into a dull, seedy marrow with tough skin, and overripe fruit left on the plant signals it to slow new production, so frequent picking keeps a plant cropping.
harvest_ready_beginner: Pick zucchini while it is still small, about 6 to 8 inches long, with shiny skin. Round kinds are best picked at about the size of a tennis ball. Zucchini grows surprisingly fast, so check your plants every day or two, it can go from small to oversized in just a couple of days. Cut the stem with a knife instead of pulling. If you leave squash on the plant too long it gets big, tough, and seedy, and the plant slows down. Picking often keeps more squash coming.
pollinator_notes_seasoned: Zucchini is monoecious: each plant carries separate male and female flowers, so a single plant sets fruit with no second variety needed. The flowers are insect-pollinated, mostly by bees, and pollen must move from the male to the female blooms. Poor pollination, common in cool, wet, or pollinator-scarce conditions, shows up as small fruit that yellow and rot at the blossom end, or as misshapen, pinched squash. Early-season male flowers often open and drop before the first females appear, which is normal. Plant flowers nearby and avoid spraying open blooms to keep pollinators working, and hand-pollinate with a small brush if fruit set stalls.
pollinator_notes_beginner: Each zucchini plant has both male and female flowers, so you only need one plant to get fruit. Bees move the pollen between flowers, so anything that brings bees to your garden helps. If your early squash stay small and rot at the tip, the flowers usually were not pollinated well, often in cool or rainy weather. It tends to sort itself out as more flowers open and bees get busy.
